articles.title: US midterm elections – a referendum on Trump
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
After a positive start, US equities turned lower and closed in negative territory yesterday (Nasdaq -1.1% and S&P 500 -0.5%). A sharp fall in oil prices (see below) failed to offset the decline, which was driven by concerns about the tech sector. The dollar weakened against the euro, while US long-term yields edged lower. After the close, Apple reported higher-than-expected third-quarter earnings of USD 2.10 per share, while revenue from China disappointed.
Oil prices fell sharply
, by almost 8%, on hopes of negotiations following reports that Iran’s supreme leader had opened the door to indirect talks with the US. Brent is now trading at around USD 105 per barrel. For an analysis of oil prices, read more 
here
. Reports of possible US strikes after the midterm elections continue to circulate, but Trump has also signalled that he wants to give diplomacy more time. Meanwhile, the US carried out a strike on the Iranian island of Qeshm yesterday, showing that the conflict is far from resolved.
Russian and Ukrainian delegations
 are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11 to discuss an end to the war in Ukraine. The US will mediate between the two countries. According to US envoy Witkoff, the talks will focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian efforts, among other issues.
Australia’s central bank, the RBA,
 raised its policy rate as expected this morning for the fifth time this year, to 4.85%, to curb inflation. Asian equities have mostly declined. Japanese markets are closed today. Equity futures point to somewhat mixed openings in the US and declines in Europe.
The US goes to the polls in the midterm elections today
. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats are at stake. The Democrats are favourites to take control of both chambers of Congress. Betting markets put the probability of a Democratic victory at 96% in the House and 74% in the Senate. The outcome could be known by Wednesday morning, Swedish time. If the result is close, counting could take another day or more. 
Yesterday, the US ISM manufacturing index showed stronger-than-expected sentiment in October. Today also brings the JOLTS labour market survey for September. Demand for labour has softened, but without any clear increase in voluntary resignations. This is consistent with a labour market in which companies are cautious about hiring but retain existing staff.
Today, our Nordic Outlook Update series turns to
 the three Baltic countries – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – as well as Finland. Through Tuesday, November 10, we are publishing our forecasts and macroeconomic views for individual countries and regions on our 
Research website
.
Nordic key stories
Another vote on a new Swedish prime minister.
 Today, parliament votes on Centre Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist as prime minister of a centrist coalition comprising the Centre Party, Social Democrats, Liberals, Christian Democrats and Greens. Her nomination is expected to be rejected, and negotiations on forming a new government appear to be progressing slowly.
Swedish wage increases of 3.9%
 under a one-year agreement are being demanded by Sweden’s industrial trade unions. The unions are also seeking provisions for shorter working hours. Past experience suggests that they could secure about 75% of their initial wage demands, equivalent to around 3%. Any wage drift would come on top of this. However, both the economy and the labour market are undergoing major changes that could affect the final outcome.

articles.title: Mellanårsval i USA – en folkomröstning om Trump
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Efter en positiv start vände USA-börserna nedåt och stängde på minus igår (Nasdaq -1,1% och S&P 500 -0,5%). Ett kraftigt fall i oljepriset (se nedan) lyckades inte motverka nedgången, som drevs av oro för tekniksektorn.
Dollarn försvagades mot euron medan amerikanska långräntor gick ned något. Apple rapporterade efter börsstängningen en högre vinst än väntat, på 2,10 USD per aktie under tredje kvartalet, samtidigt som intäkterna från Kina var en besvikelse.
Oljepriset föll kraftigt
 på förhandlingsförhoppningar, med nästan 8%, efter uppgifter om att Irans högsta ledare öppnat för indirekta samtal med USA. Brentpriset ligger nu runt 105 USD per fat. För en analys av oljepriset, läs mer 
här
. Uppgifter om möjliga amerikanska anfall efter mellanårsvalet förekommer fortsatt, men Trump har också signalerat att han vill ge diplomatin mer tid. Samtidigt genomförde USA en attack mot den iranska ön Qeshm under gårdagen, vilket visar att konflikten är långt ifrån löst.
Ryssland och Ukraina
 ska mötas på tjänstemannanivå i Abu Dhabi mellan den 10 och 11 november för att diskutera ett krigsslut i Ukraina. USA ska agera som medlare mellan länderna och enligt USA:s sändebud Witkoff ska fokus ligga på säkerhetsarrangemang efter kriget, nedtrappning, humanitära insatser etc.
Australiens centralbank, RBA,
 höjde som väntat styrräntan nu på morgonen för femte gången i år, till 4,85%, för att dämpa inflationen. I Asien har börserna mestadels gått ned. De japanska marknaderna är stängda idag. Börsterminerna indikerar något blandade öppningar i USA och nedgångar i Europa.
USA går till mellanårsval idag
. Samtliga 435 platser i representanthuset och 35 av senatens platser står på spel. Demokraterna är favoriter att ta kontroll över båda kamrarna i kongressen. Enligt bettingmarknaden är sannolikheten 96% för en seger för Demokraterna i representanthuset, och 74% i senaten. Valresultatet kan bli klart under onsdagsmorgonen svensk tid. Vid ett jämnt resultat kan rösträkningen ta ytterligare en eller flera dagar. Min kollega Elisabet skriver mer om valet 
här
.
Igår visade det amerikanska inköpschefsindexet ISM ett bättre stämningsläge än väntat inom industrin i oktober. Idag publiceras även arbetsmarknadsundersökningen JOLTS för september. Efterfrågan på arbetskraft har dämpats, men utan någon tydlig ökning av frivilliga uppsägningar. Det är förenligt med en arbetsmarknad där företagen är försiktiga med anställningar men behåller befintlig personal.
I vår serie av Nordic Outlook Updates
 har turen idag kommit till de tre baltiska länderna, Estland, Lettland och Litauen samt Finland. Fram till tisdagen den 10 november publicerar vi löpande våra prognoser och vår syn på den makroekonomiska utvecklingen i enskilda länder och regioner på vår 
Researchsida.
Sverige
Ny statsministeromröstning
. Idag röstar riksdagen om Centerpartiets partiledare Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist som statsminister i en mittenregering bestående av C, S, L, KD och MP. Hon väntas röstas ned och än så länge verkar förhandlingarna om en ny regering gå trögt.
Löneökningar på 3,9%
 i ett ettårigt avtal kräver fackförbunden inom industrin. Facken kräver också avsättningar för kortare arbetstid. Historien indikerar att facken skulle kunna få igenom ca 75% av det man kräver initialt. Det skulle motsvara runt 3%. Därtill kommer eventuell löneglidning. Samtidigt genomgår både ekonomin och arbetsmarknaden stora förändringar som kan påverka slutresultatet.

articles.title: Nordic Outlook Update - Latvia
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Eng)
articles.fulltext:
Analyst: Dainis Gašpuitis
Our publication of Nordic Outlook in November has a slightly different format compared to other editions during the year. Under the heading Nordic Outlook Update , we are continuously publishing our forecasts and our macro view for individual countries/regions. On Tuesday 10 November, we will publish our overall view on growth, inflation, interest rates, etc., together with the table of all forecasts. 
The economic momentum is strong, and growth is expected to be the highest in almost a decade, excluding the post-pandemic rebound in 2021. This expansion is driven by a recovery in household consumption, resilient goods exports and rising investment. However, economic growth is expected to moderate to around 2 per cent in 2027 and 2028, partly due to weaker consumption as a result of higher inflation and interest rates.
A benchmark revision has reassessed the entire national accounts time series dating back to 2018. The revisions increased GDP growth rates by 0.5 and 0.3 percentage points in 2024 and 2025 respectively. For 2026 growth rates in the first and second quarters are 0.2 and 0.5 percentage points higher.
Due to a stronger than expected recovery during the first half of the year, we are raising the 2026 growth rate to 3 per. Following this year's strong growth, we expect growth to slow in 2027-2028. Household consumption is likely to be constrained by rising inflation. Higher interest rates, combined with the conclusion of the current EU funding cycle, are expected to slow investment growth. Fiscal consolidation will also weigh on economic activity.
Higher energy prices continued to be the main driver of inflation, though partly offset by lower food prices. While the pass-through of energy costs has so far been limited, it’s expected to feed into heating tariffs and services. The extent of second-round effects will depend on how long energy prices remain elevated, suggesting a further increase in inflation in the coming months.
Average wages rose by 4.3 per cent in the second quarter, but data confirms earlier signals that the growth rate is slowing somewhat faster than expected. Part of this can be attributed to a sharper deceleration in public sector wage growth (2.1 per cent, compared with 5.4 per cent in the private sector). Given the pressure on public finances, this gap in favour of the private sector is likely to persist, suggesting that wage growth rate will remain in the 4.5–5.5 per cent range over the coming years.
The recovery in household consumption has been remarkably resilient despite rising energy prices. Moreover, consumer confidence improved further in Q3. However, higher inflation will hold back purchasing power and consumer spending going forward.
There has been exceptional activity in the housing market, with strong growth in house prices, transaction volumes and lending. However, rising uncertainty, higher inflation and interest rates suggest a moderation in the activity, particularly early next year.

articles.title: Nordic Outlook Update - Lithuania
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Eng)
articles.fulltext:
Analyst: Tadas Povilauskas
Our publication of Nordic Outlook in November has a slightly different format compared to other editions during the year. Under the heading Nordic Outlook Update , we are continuously publishing our forecasts and our macro view for individual countries/regions. On Tuesday 10 November, we will publish our overall view on growth, inflation, interest rates, etc., together with the table of all forecasts. 
Household consumption and services exports are driving economic growth in 2026. As the impact of withdrawals from second-pillar pension funds fades, household consumption and, consequently, economic growth are expected to slow next year. Investment growth is also set to moderate. Inflation is expected to ease only slightly, while the rapidly rising public debt is becoming an increasing concern.  
GDP grew by 2.8 per cent year-on-year in the first three quarters of 2026. Growth is expected to weaken in the final quarter, driven primarily by decelerating household consumption. We maintain our GDP growth forecasts for 2027 and 2028 at 2.1 per cent and 2.7 per cent, respectively, as consumption growth strengthens.
Around 50 per cent of eligible participants have withdrawn assets from the second-pillar pension funds, in total the equivalent to 5.1 per cent of GDP. As anticipated, only up to 5 per cent of these funds have been reinvested in other savings instruments, while one quarter has been withdrawn as cash. However, household consumption growth has so far been weaker than expected, as a large share of the funds remains in current or term-deposit accounts.
Consumer confidence is expected to soften as annual inflation remains above 6 per cent in the coming months. The government refrained from introducing substantial measures to cushion this autumn's rise in energy prices; consequently, diesel prices are among the highest in the region and due to higher energy prices, we have raised our 2027 inflation forecast significantly to 4.4 per cent. Meanwhile, we expect service inflation to moderate somewhat.
The labour market remains resilient, characterized by slightly lower unemployment and somewhat higher employment. However, employment in sectors such as ICT is already significantly below last year's level, which may provide an early indication that AI-driven productivity gains are beginning to weigh on labour demand. Wage growth has been surprisingly strong, prompting us to raise our forecast for wage growth in 2026. We expect wage growth to slow in 2027, reflecting a smaller increase in the minimum wage, cooling public-sector wage growth, and weaker overall economic activity.
Despite numerous challenges, manufacturing output continues to expand, outperforming many other EU countries. Although the share of energy-intensive industries has declined, the recent surge in energy prices will pressure many producers. Private investment remains resilient, but rising construction costs and elevated interest rates are likely to weigh increasingly on investment in the coming years.
The government has presented a draft central government budget projecting a deficit of 3.7 per cent of GDP in 2027, significantly exceeding previous expectations. This partly reflects a sharp increase in defence spending without a corresponding rise in government revenue. Absent new revenue measures or offsetting expenditure cuts, the budget deficit is poised to widen further in the coming years.

articles.title: Nordic Outlook Update - Estonia
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Eng)
articles.fulltext:
Analyst: Mihkel Nestor
Our publication of Nordic Outlook in November has a slightly different format compared to other editions during the year. Under the heading Nordic Outlook Update , we are continuously publishing our forecasts and our macro view for individual countries/regions. On Tuesday 10 November, we will publish our overall view on growth, inflation, interest rates, etc., together with the table of all forecasts. 
The economic recovery has continued broadly as expected, supported by both stronger household consumption and a rebound in exports. However, higher inflation and interest rates cast a shadow over the coming quarters. Rising prices will weigh on real wage growth and consumer sentiment, while higher interest rates will dampen demand as growth slows important export markets. We lower our GDP forecast for next year to 2.2 per cent and expect growth to pick up to close to 3 per cent in 2028.  
Recent GDP figures show that the economy expanded by 0.6 per cent in the third quarter. This is broadly the same pace as average growth in the previous two quarters.
Significant revisions to the national accounts at the end of August showed that the economy was also in better shape than previously thought, with GDP growth for 2025 revised up to 1.3 per cent.
The strong upswing in household consumption in the first quarter of 2026, driven by changes to personal income taxation, faded in subsequent months, but retail sales have continued to grow at a steady pace. However, rising interest rates and inflation will curb growth in 2027.
Household consumption has benefited from the lowest inflation in years. The average HICP inflation in 2026 will end up around 3 per cent, although surging energy prices have pushed it back above that level. Elevated fuel prices will keep inflation at 3 per cent also in 2027.
While consumer sentiment had been recovering from very low levels for most of 2026, the recent rise in energy prices has pushed it lower again. Business sentiment is stronger in export-oriented manufacturing, where growth has been gathering pace.
The labour market has remained stable, with the unemployment rate falling to around 5 per cent, its lowest level since before the pandemic. Wage growth has remained close to 6 per cent, roughly in line with nominal GDP growth. We expect the labour market to remain stable over the forecast horizon.
The surge in new lending to businesses has yet to translate into stronger investment activity. The prospect of higher interest rates will keep businesses cautious in the coming quarters.
The March 2027 parliamentary elections are expected to bring a new governing coalition to power. Despite promises to lower taxes, including abolishing the unpopular car tax and cutting VAT on food, the scope for such measures remains limited, given an already large budget deficit of close to 4 per cent.

articles.title: Nordic Outlook Update - Finland
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Eng)
articles.fulltext:
Analyst: Mihkel Nestor
Our publication of Nordic Outlook in November has a slightly different format compared to other editions during the year. Under the heading Nordic Outlook Update , we are continuously publishing our forecasts and our macro view for individual countries/regions. On Tuesday 10 November, we will publish our overall view on growth, inflation, interest rates, etc., together with the table of all forecasts. 
The Finnish economy has continued to outperform the gloomy expectations prevailing at the beginning of the year. However, recent revisions to the national accounts suggest that the rebound has been less pronounced than previously estimated. While higher inflation and interest rates pose risks to the recovery, we expect GDP to grow by 1.8 per cent in 2027, followed by a more moderate 1.5 per cent in 2028.  
Economic growth has continued to gain momentum with quarterly growth averaging 0.5 per cent so far in 2026. However, these figures should be treated with some caution, as earlier estimates of strong growth have been revised down.
The biggest contributor to growth has been the strong performance in the export sector. Exports were already doing well in 2025 and have continued to gather pace since then, culminating in a remarkable 9.4 per cent annual increase in the second quarter of 2026. Exports have been boosted by strong demand for a broad range of machinery and equipment, as well as ships. Demand has also improved in the traditionally important wood and pulp industries. Strong order books suggest that exports should continue to perform well in 2027.
The pick-up in retail sales and household demand that started at the very end of 2025 has continued to gather pace. Despite high unemployment, relatively moderate inflation and earlier collective bargaining agreements have supported faster real wage growth.
Labour market rigidities have created stark contrasts: while unemployment remains at 10.5 per cent, the highest rate in the EU, wage growth is expected to average around 3.5 per cent this year. Despite an acceleration in economic activity, bringing unemployment down will take time, as employers remain cautious about hiring in the current highly uncertain environment.
Economic confidence has improved across sectors throughout 2026, but the surge in energy prices has hit consumer confidence hard this autumn, also weighing on confidence in retail trade and services. These trends could lead to somewhat weaker household consumption in the coming quarters.
The real estate and construction sectors continue to lag far behind the rest of the economy. However, prices are now likely to stabilise, raising hopes of a gradual recovery in construction and sales.
The greatest risk to the economic recovery comes from interest rates. Both Finnish domestic demand and exports tend to be highly sensitive to interest rates. Persistently elevated rates could once again weigh on exports and dampen domestic demand.

articles.title: Calibrating the NOK FRA fly
articles.heading: Norway 360
articles.fulltext:
Norway 360 – Weekly Market (Re)View Norway 360 provides you with a quick and broad overview of Norwegian macro, rates and FX. *** See attachment for full report ***
Macro highlights: 
Norges Bank’s interim decision on Nov 5
Norges Bank is widely expected to leave its policy rate unchanged at 4.50%. The Sep rate path did not include any probability of a hike at this meeting and there have been limited new data released since the Sep MPR. 
Minutes from the September meeting indicated divergent views among board members. Reversing last year’s two rate cuts while signaling a “high for longer” approach appears as a fine-tuned compromise. It also suggests that the bar for raising the policy rate further is high unless the inflation outlook deteriorates materially. 
Data since September do not deviate substantially from projections. External price pressures appear higher, but this is reflected in a stronger NOK. Overall, risks to inflation remain skewed to the upside, but we believe the Committee will await more data before reassessing the policy outlook. Hence, we expect the Committee to repeat its ‘high for longer’ guidance while simultaneously reiterate a readiness to act if necessary. 
The market does not discount any likelihood of a move on Thursday but sees close to a 50/50 chance of a hike in Dec and a policy rate peak of 4.70% next spring. Our expectations of a reiteration of the Sep guidance suggest limited market moves, and any initial reaction in the NOK should be short-lived.
Rates highlights (I): Front-end view – calibrating the NOK ‘FRA fly’ 
Our main view remains that the NOK FRA curve should have more potential to invert (Jun27/Jun28
) – a catalyst would obviously be a global disinflation impulse from the energy complex. 
We have been pairing this flattener view with a front micro steepener (Dec26/March27) 
as ‘hedge’ on continued rates sell-off and that central banks may have to do more – 
we now roll this ‘micro steepener’ to March27/Jun27 
which is about flat. This should be safe under the assumption that Norges Bank will not be cutting by summer 2027. Rolling into Mar27/Dec27 also avoids any uncertain year-end effects in FRA-OIS that is unrelated to Norges Bank pricing.
Should Norges bank hike in Dec and/or March (18bps cumulatively priced) we assume that the curve would invert more into 2028 while March27/June27 would fail to invert much and price an ‘on hold’ period.
Rates highlights (II): 
Potential for 5Y5Y/10Y10Y steepening on back of seasonality
The NOK 5Y5Y/10Y10Y tends to flatten during times of long-end issuance 
(e.g., spring & 
autumn
) – as it gets swapped (receiving long swaps). 
Last 
autumn
 was an outlier 
as we didn’t see the normal seasonal flattening of the long-end, possibly due to the steepening in Europe. 
This year, however, some seasonality appears to be back in play 
– however it is also helped by the EUR curve (10Y10Y spread to Euro has been stable while Euro curve flattened).
We expect volumes in fixed rate issuance to moderate towards month-end. Absent continued flattening pressures on the Euribor curve, bias is to be paid this area, although the case is not as strong as in 2023 or 2022.
In contrast to previous seasonal episode the potential is more moderate at say +25bps in 5Y5Y/10Y10Y into February
.
FX highlights (I): 
Norges Bank’s FX transactions: a new SEB framework established
A new SEB framework aims to forecast what Norges Bank will announce as their daily FX transactions in the coming month and making changes more transparent. The framework has recently been established, and chart 1 shows what the model would have estimated throughout the year, based on publicly available information at the time. The model does a good job directionally 
and also
 has a reasonably good historical fit. 
Chart 2 shows the contributing factors behind the changes in the monthly amounts in 2026. Unsurprisingly, changes in petroleum tax and the non-oil budget deficit are the main drivers behind the changes.
Our model indicated that an increase in FX purchases in Nov (from NOK 300 to 750mn/d) would be appropriate if one assumed that Norges Bank accepted revised 2026 numbers for the non-oil budget deficit, as shown in the 2027 budget proposal. This would have led to a NOK 16.4bn drop in the non-oil deficit, and a smaller need to have NOK to fund the deficit (hence higher NOK sales/FX purchases).
Norges Bank left purchases unchanged, however. This might be an indication that Norges Bank awaits the formal parliamentary approval of the budget before they accept the government’s number for their transactions. Adjusting our model in line with this assumption, we arrive at unchanged numbers as well (though with a 50mn diff). For explanations behind Norges Bank’s transactions, and details on our framework, see 
here
.
FX highlights (I) cont.:Norges Bank’s FX transactions: NOK impact is decided by the deficit and dependent on timing.
Norges Bank's FX transactions have drawn a lot of attention due to its potential impact on the NOK. 
Timing mismatch:
 The impact mainly stems from timing mismatches between flows, and 
in particular related
 to petroleum taxes. Oil companies are active in the market daily to buy NOK ahead of tax installments and can quickly adopt to large swings in oil and gas prices. Though Norges Bank’s flow is offsetting this effect, they come with a lag as the bank is largely dependent on public information and revises their transactions only once a month. 
Net NOK inflows: 
Ultimately, what matters for the krone is the size of the non-oil budget deficit. This determines the amount of NOK that actually ‘stays in the economy’, and the change in the deficit from one year to another represents the net inflow of NOK from the petroleum mechanism. For 2026, this implied a NOK 21bn NOK-outflow, while the 2027 budget proposal implies a NOK 107bn NOK-inflow.
What comes in goes out: 
In practice, however, the impact is much smaller as a widening non-oil budget deficit is mirrored in a wider mainland trade deficit. Consequently, much of the petroleum revenue spent domestically ultimately leaks out through higher imports.
FX highlights (II): 
We remain bearish on NOKSEK in the medium-term – near-term dependent on escalation/diplomacy.
Upcoming data & events:
Existing home prices (Wed) rose more than expected in Sep, up 0.3% m/m (SA) vs. Norges Bank’s 0.1% forecast. We expect prices to rise modestly towards year-end, and regard Norges Bank’s full-year estimate of 3.0% to be reasonable. 
The highlight of the week is Norges Bank’s rate decision (Thu) where both we and consensus expect an unchanged policy rate of 4.50% and little forward guidance. We expect the Bank to await more data before reassessing the policy outlook and repeat its “high for longer” message. 
Manufacturing production (Fri) declined in Aug, leaving the Jul-Aug broadly unchanged from the Q2, offering little directional guidance for manufacturing production in Q3.

articles.title: Nordic Outlook Update - United Kingdom
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Eng)
articles.fulltext:
Our publication of Nordic Outlook in November has a slightly different format compared to other editions during the year. Under the heading Nordic Outlook Update , we are continuously publishing our forecasts and our macro view for individual countries/regions. On Tuesday 10 November, we will publish our overall view on growth, inflation, interest rates, etc., together with the table of all forecasts. 
The UK economy has exceeded expectations this year, but the energy shock is pushing inflation towards 3.5–4 per cent, which threatens the recovery. We expect the Bank of England to hike in November, possibly again in February, but do not see these moves as the start of another tightening cycle. The Autumn Budget prioritized household support but remained cautious, which calmed the markets. The hard spending choices, such as defence and social care, are left for 2027.  
The economy has been stronger than expected. GDP grew by 0.6 per cent in Q1 and 0.5 per cent in Q2, and monthly data pointed to a third solid quarter. The composite PMI rose to an eight-month high of 53. Following the strong first half, we raise our growth forecast for 2026 by 0.3 per centage points to 1.4 per cent. 
Increasing
 headwinds in 2027. Energy and borrowing costs are squeezing households, mortgage approvals have fallen to a three year low, and house prices have stalled. The Office for Budget Responsibility has cut its 2027 growth forecast to 1.0 per cent from 1.6 per cent, and household consumption remains the decisive factor. 
Labour-market conditions are weaker than headline figures imply. Despite unemployment falling to 4.7 per cent, payroll employment is down 111,000 annually. Private-sectors’ pay growth of 3.0 per cent is compatible with the inflation target, though upside risks remain. 
Inflation rose to 3.5 per cent in September, with services inflation at 3.7 per cent. The BoE expects inflation to be slightly above 4 per cent in early 2027, and the OBR has raised its 2027 forecast to 3.4 per cent. We believe inflation will peak in early 2027, before gradually coming back to target. 
We expect the BoE to hike on 5 November. Markets price in around four hikes in total, which we consider too hawkish. Depending on energy prices and their economic impact, another hike could follow, possibly in February. However, we do not see this as the start of a renewed tightening cycle.
Chancellor Healey's first budget did no harm. The £11.6bn package, mainly supporting households and partly funded by doubling the bank surcharge, left 
fiscal 
headroom at £15bn, down from £23.6bn in March. Spending is front-loaded and tightening back-loaded, as is 
typical of
 UK budgets. 
Decisions
 on defence and social care spending 
await
 the 2027 Spending Review.
The gilt market has calmed somewhat. The 10-year yield is 5.3 per cent, down from 5.5 per cent in early October
. Cutting
 long-dated issuance to 6.2 per cent of planned sales has helped flatten the curve. 
Hawkish BoE
 expectations 
have supported sterling
, with EUR/GBP at 0.83 
versus
 0.86 in August, and GBP/USD at 1.34.
Government spending and strong investment growth have offset stagnant household consumption. Reviving household demand remains key to achieving a broader recovery.

articles.title: New attacks on Iran will lead to nowhere and the cost would be high
articles.heading: Crude oil comment
articles.fulltext:
Trump gives diplomacy another chance after oil spiked on Friday.
 The Brent Jan-27 contract rose 1.6% last week. It traded in a range of $109.02 - 114.29/b and closed the week at $113.43/b while. The Brent Dec-26 contract rolled off on Friday with a close of $117.64/b. There was some softening in physical crude prices. Physical premiums for Fortis and Oseberg fell further to $5.9/b and $1.9/b after having reached unusual highs of $20/b recently. The Dated Brent crude oil price still closed at a strong $118.77/b. The Brent Jan-27 contract is down 3.3% this morning to $100.8/b as Trump has indicated that he will give diplomacy another chance. As a result the elevated risk premium in Brent crude lately is partially erased this morning as an imminent attack post 3 November seems to have been averted for now.
New attacks by the US/Israel will lead to nowhere.
 There are hectic diplomatic efforts in the Middle East to avert a new US/Israeli attack on Iran. None of the Gulf countries want another round of hostilities. The US didn't seek support for this war from any of its allies (except Israel). Not even its Gulf allies were consulted. The US is now in a quagmire in the Middle East with little support to be found anywhere except from Israel. The Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said on Saturday that: "A second round will be more dangerous, more destructive and it will lead to nowhere" 
(Bloomberg story yesterday)
. And that is precisely it. A new round of attacks on Iran by the US and Israel will lead to nowhere politically. Trump is hoping or maybe praying that a new, large attack on Iran will soften Iran so it bends to the will of the US and Israel. That is just as fancifully thinking as Putin now is pursuing through its attacks on civilians in Ukraine.
Iran is well prepared to retaliate and "there will be no geographical limitations".
 Iran was heavily attack in March and April with US-Israeli attacking military targets across Iran. Since then it has only been briefer and more limited attacks like in June and 1 September. The latter lasted only 10 hours. Iran has essentially been able to rebuild and reestablish a lot of its defensive and offensive capabilities almost for a full 6 months. Iran has naturally not been standing still as it naturally has expected and prepared for renewed attacks by the US and Iran. Naturally since Trump has continuously threatened to do so. Iran is assumed to still hold 3/4 of its prewar ammunition. The Gulf states and the US has burned off a major share of its defensive rockets (Patriots and Thaad) which are needed to counter Iranian ballistic rockets. Iran however likely still has a large stock of ballistic rockets in store. Attacking Iran again now is a much bigger risk and much more dangerous than attacking it for example in May. The Gulf countries probably understands this very well. Trump hopefully also understands this. Iranian media stated this weekend that if Iran is attacked it will retaliate without geographical limitations. 
One last attack and then a declaration of victory?
 We struggle to see any good reason for why the US would choose to attack Iran again. We totally agree with Badr Abdlatty above: "it will lead to nowhere". Senior researcher, Karen Young, at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy has a different angle: "I think we will see a US-Israel attack on Iran, a declaration of victory, and a deal that is favorable to Iran". I.e. another attack is essentially a process to pack up and leave. We'll see.
Infrastructure damage or surplus?
 The risk of a new attack and widespread Gulf energy infrastructure damage continues to hang over the market. It would send oil prices sharply higher. However, if it doesn't happen, then the global oil market will instead face a surplus and much lower oil prices. Or as Mike McGlone in Bloomberg argues: "Worsening conditions in the Russia-Ukraine and US-Iran wars is needed to avoid Brent crude from reverting to $60/b he argues".

articles.title: Lower oil prices and rising stock markets ahead of the US election
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
US equities initially continued to fall on Friday evening
, but subsequently recovered and ended at roughly the same levels as when European markets closed (note that the Swedish market closed early on Friday). AI-related concerns were the main driver, with the Nasdaq falling almost 3% and the S&P 500 losing just under 2%. Risk appetite has returned over the weekend, with equity futures in both the US and Europe pointing higher, while Asian stock markets are rising. A statement from Trump that he wants to give diplomacy another chance (in the Middle East) is contributing to a decline in oil prices of almost USD 4 per barrel, reversing last week's increase. Brent crude is now trading at just under USD 110 per barrel.
Despite the rise in oil prices, market expectations for central bank rate hikes declined last week.
 One reason may be that higher oil prices have not translated into higher petrol and diesel prices. On the contrary, petrol prices in particular have fallen. However, slightly less hawkish central banks and unchanged policy rates in October are probably more important explanations. The yield spread between France and Germany has started to widen again following the narrowing triggered by Moody's decision to leave France's credit rating unchanged, although it remains some way below its peak of 175 basis points.
There are several interesting data releases this week, but tomorrow's US elections will be the main focus.
 A Democratic majority in the House of Representatives is widely expected, and according to Polymarket, there is also a high probability (just over 70%) that the Democrats will take control of the Senate. If the Democrats gain control of both chambers of Congress, Trump's ability to implement his policies will be constrained, although he will retain considerable influence over trade, immigration and foreign policy. Moreover, the president can veto almost any legislation that does not have the support of two-thirds of members in both the House and the Senate. It is not unusual for presidents to lose control of Congress in midterm elections, and the US always manages to keep functioning despite often substantial political disagreements. Friday's US labour market report and Norges Bank's policy rate decision are other highlights this week. 
We will continue publishing Nordic Outlook Updates throughout the week
, with updated forecasts for individual countries. Today, it is the turn of the euro area and the UK. You can find these and much more on 
our 
Research page
.
Nordic key stories
Growth in Sweden remained strong in the third quarter
, at least according to the not always reliable flash GDP estimate. Strong growth is also supported by several other indicators, and we believe that GDP growth could be revised up slightly when the more comprehensive figures are published on 27 November. However, a sharp decline in household confidence in last week's NIER survey is a warning signal, and the risks to our optimistic growth forecast are clearly tilted to the downside. Energy prices are expected to rise significantly over the next 3–4 months, while the Riksbank's rate hikes will quickly put additional pressure on many highly indebted households. There is a significant risk that consumer confidence will continue to deteriorate and consumption will slow. SEB's Housing Price Indicator, released this morning, fell by 5 index points to 38. This is a relatively modest decline by historical standards, and the level still suggests that house prices will continue to rise. However, there is also a significant risk that the indicator will decline further in the coming months. Read more 
here
.
We expect Swedish CPIF inflation excluding energy to slow to 0.4% year-on-year in October
 (from 0.5%), slightly below the consensus estimate. Relatively warm weather in October caused electricity prices to fall somewhat, and we expect energy prices to have increased only modestly during the month, contributing to a decline in headline CPIF inflation to 1.4% from 1.5%. However, electricity prices are expected to rise significantly in November and December, while a normalisation of taxes will push fuel prices up by 15% in December. As a result, CPIF inflation looks set to reach 2.7% year-on-year in December. Read more about our expectations ahead of Thursday's flash estimate
 here.
Almost everyone expects the Riksbank to raise its policy rate on Wednesday
, and the most interesting aspect will probably be what the Executive Board says about the outlook. We expect the message to be that the September rate path, which signals just under two additional hikes next year, remains valid. However, our rate survey shows that opinions are divided, with half of respondents expecting the Riksbank to signal that upside risks have increased. 
Read more about our expectations 
here
 and about the interest rate survey 
here
.  
DI's Shadow Monetary Policy Committee also favours a rate hike in November but recommends proceeding cautiously thereafter. 
Read more 
here
. (Swedish pay link).  
Tomorrow, the Swedish Riksdag will vote on Centre Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist as prime minister
, but she is widely expected to lose the vote. For now, there appears to be no breakthrough in negotiations to form a new government.
Norges Bank is widely expected to leave its policy rate unchanged at 4.50%
 at its upcoming meeting. We expect the Bank to emphasise continued uncertainty surrounding underlying inflation and the risk that elevated external price pressures could slow disinflation. Nevertheless, we expect little new guidance on the policy outlook. As this is an interim meeting, no new forecasts will be published. 
More about Norges Bank 
here
.

articles.title: Lägre oljepris och stigande börser inför valet i USA
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
USA-börserna fortsatte inledningsvis nedåt under fredagskvällen,
 men återhämtade sig och slutade på ungefär samma nivåer som vid stängningen i Europa (notera att Sverige stängde tidigt i fredags). Oro kring AI var den främsta drivkraften och Nasdaq föll med nästan 3%, medan S&P 500 tappade knappt 2%. Under helgen har riskaptiten återvänt och börsterminerna i både USA och Europa pekar uppåt, samtidigt som börserna i Asien stiger. Ett uttalande från Trump om att han vill ge diplomatin en chans till (i Mellanöstern) bidrar till att oljepriset faller med nästan 4 dollar per fat, vilket innebär att förra veckans uppgång har reverserats. Brentoljan kostar nu knappt 110 dollar per fat.
Trots att oljepriset har stigit minskade marknadens förväntningar på räntehöjningar 
från centralbankerna förra veckan. Ett skäl kan vara att det högre oljepriset inte har fått priserna på bensin och diesel att stiga. Tvärtom har framför allt bensinpriserna fallit. Lite mindre hökaktiga centralbanker och oförändrade styrräntor i oktober är dock antagligen en viktigare förklaring. Ränteskillnaden mellan Frankrike och Tyskland har börjat stiga igen efter nedgången som följde på att Moody’s lämnade kreditbetyget oförändrat, men det är fortfarande en bit kvar till toppnivån på 175 räntepunkter.
En hel del intressant statistik väntar under veckan, men valet i USA på i morgon kommer att stå mest i fokus.
 Alla räknar med att Demokraterna får majoritet i representanthuset och enligt Polymarket är sannolikheten hög (drygt 70%) för att Demokraterna även tar över senaten. Om Demokraterna tar kontrollen över kongressens båda kamrar kommer Trumps möjligheter att få igenom sin politik att begränsas, men han kommer att behålla stort inflytande över handels-, immigrations- och utrikespolitik. Dessutom har presidenten vetorätt mot nästan all lagstiftning som inte har stöd av två tredjedelar av ledamöterna i både representanthuset och senaten. Att presidenter får kongressen emot sig i mellanårsval är inte ovanligt, och USA lyckas alltid fortsätta fungera trots ofta stora politiska motsättningar. Amerikansk arbetsmarknadsstatistik på fredag, och räntebesked från Norges Bank, är andra höjdpunkter denna vecka. Mer om Norges Bank 
här
 och USA-valet
här.
Vi fortsätter under veckan att publicera Nordic Outlook Updates,
 med uppdaterade prognoser för olika länder. I dag har turen kommit till euroområdet och Storbritannien. Du hittar dessa och mycket annat på vår 
Researchsida
.
Sverige
Tillväxten i Sverige fortsatte att vara stark under tredje kvartalet
, i alla fall enligt det inte alltid pålitliga snabbestimatet för BNP. Att tillväxten var stark stöds också av många andra indikatorer och vi tror att tillväxten kan komma att justeras upp något när det mer genomräknade utfallet publiceras den 27 november. En tydlig nedgång i hushållens förtroende enligt KI-barometern förra veckan är dock en varningssignal och riskerna för vår i och för sig optimistiska tillväxtprognos ligger tydligt på nedsidan. Energipriserna kommer att fortsätta stiga betydligt de närmaste 3–4 månaderna och Riksbankens räntehöjningar kommer snabbt att sätta ytterligare press på många högt skuldsatta hushåll. Sannolikheten är hög att konsumentförtroendet fortsätter att falla och att konsumtionen saktar in. SEB:s Boprisindikator, som presenterades nu på morgonen, faller med 5 indexenheter till 38. Det är en ganska liten nedgång i ett historiskt perspektiv och nivån tyder fortfarande på att bostadspriserna kommer att fortsätta stiga. Risken är dock stor att även Boprisindikatorn fortsätter nedåt under de närmaste månaderna. Läs mer 
här.
Vi räknar med att KPIF exklusive energi saktade in till 0,4 procent i årstakt i oktober
 (från 0,5%), vilket är något lägre än konsensusestimatet. En ganska varm oktobermånad gjorde att elpriserna föll tillbaka något och vi räknar med att energipriserna steg relativt lite i oktober, vilket bidrar till att även KPIF-inflationen sjunker till 1,4% från 1,5%. Under november och december kommer elpriserna dock att stiga betydligt, samtidigt som en normalisering av skatterna kommer att höja drivmedelspriserna med 15% i december. Det gör att KPIF-inflationen i december ser ut att hamna på 2,7% i årstakt. Läs mer om våra förväntningar inför snabb-estimatet på torsdag 
här.
Nästan alla räknar med att styrräntan höjs på onsdag 
och mest intressant blir nog vad direktionen säger om utsikterna framöver. Vi tror att budskapet blir att räntebanan från september, som signalerar knappt två höjningar nästa år, fortfarande gäller. Vår ränteenkät visar dock att åsikterna går isär och hälften av dem som svarat tror att Riksbanken kommer att säga att riskerna på uppsidan har ökat. Läs mer om våra förväntningar 
här
 och om ränteenkäten 
här
. DI:s skuggdirektion vill också normalisera räntan i november men gå försiktigt fram därefter. Läs mer 
här
. (betallänk).
Imorgon röstar riksdagen om Centerledaren
, Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, som statsminister, men alla räknar med att hon förlorar. Någon öppning i förhandlingarna om en ny regering verkar inte finnas i nuläget.

articles.title: Weakening housing price sentiment
articles.heading: SEB Housing Price Indicator (Sweden)
articles.fulltext:
The SEB Housing Price Indicator fell again in November as fewer respondents expect prices to rise. Housing market sentiment has followed a choppy downward trend over the past few months. The decline in November is in line with the latest reading for overall consumer confidence, which dropped markedly as headwinds intensify ahead of the winter. Nevertheless, housing price sentiment remains above its historical average.
Key points
Home price sentiment 
falls by 
5 index points to 38 in November.
Weaker trajectory in line with consumer confidence, 
but
 much 
less pronounced.
Plans to fix 
mortgage 
rates 
continue
 to gain ground
.
Housing
 market sentiment has been relatively stable for 
an extended period
 and has remained above 
its
 historical average for more than a year. However, the November survey 
shows signs of a weakening trend. Households’ home price sentiment has long been stronger than overall consumer confidence. Over the past two months, consumer confidence has fluctuated sharply. Together with softer housing market sentiment, these movements suggest that near-term headwinds from higher energy and mortgage costs are starting to weigh on households. Read more in our comment on the NIER survey 
here
.
The lower 
indicator 
reading in November was mainly driven by a 
smaller share of respondents expecting prices to rise (from 53% in October to 49% in November).
November’s
 survey 
shows respondents preparing for higher policy rates, as plans to fix mortgage rates become more common—a pattern we typically see in this survey. However, as we have noted previously,
 mortgage bond yields have already moved 
considerably
 higher.

articles.title: Nordic Outlook Update - Euro area
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Eng)
articles.fulltext:
Our publication of Nordic Outlook in November has a slightly different format compared to other editions during the year. Under the heading Nordic Outlook Update , we are continuously publishing our forecasts and our macro view for individual countries/regions. On Tuesday 10 November, we will publish our overall view on growth, inflation, interest rates, etc., together with the table of all forecasts. 
Stronger-than-expected growth so far in 2026 will be followed by a temporary slowdown in the end of the year and early 2027. Growth will be supported by household consumption and investment. Higher energy prices will keep inflation elevated for longer, prompting the ECB to raise interest rates in December 2026 and March 2027. As inflation moves closer to target, the ECB will cut rates three times in 2028. Elections in several countries – with parties on the fringes gaining ground – can have major implications for the whole of the EU.  
Indicators such as the PMI point to stronger economic activity while consumer confidence remains low (and weaker than actual consumer behaviour suggests). GDP growth has been resilient so far in 2026, prompting us to an upward revise of our forecast for 2026. However, quarterly growth is expected to slow at the end of 2026 and early 2027 due to higher interest rates and elevated energy prices, in particular natural gas.  
GDP is projected to grow just above 1 per cent in 2026 and slightly below 1.5 per cent in 2027–2028. A solid labour market and rising real disposable income supports consumption. Investment in infrastructure, defence, and to some extent AI, will also support growth. 
The political situation remains highly uncertain, especially in France. Public finances are weak, and substantial fiscal consolidation is needed. At the same time, large-scale demonstrations over poor conditions in schools and economic hardship are adding to pressure for higher public spending. French budget deficit is expected to reach almost 5.5 per cent of GDP this year and the government aims for it to reach around 5 per cent in 2027. However, the weak growth outlook makes this forecast appear rather optimistic. In polls for the presidential election in 2027, far-right and far-left candidate are gaining ground. 
To lift growth above potential around 1.2 per cent the EU needs to make further progress on the reforms proposed in the 2024 Draghi report. Deepening the single market, particularly by integrating capital markets and simplifying regulation, could lift growth.
Energy prices remain high, with price increases broadening this autumn and pushing home energy costs higher. There are still no clear signs of indirect or second-round effects on core inflation, but we expect these to start feeding through in 2027. The extent of these effects will depend on the situation in the Middle East. A resolution of the conflict could ease price pressures and will be key to the inflation outlook for 2028 and for the ECB.
The ECB is concerned about elevated energy prices, indirect effects and second-round effects on wages. If energy prices fall, as markets expect, the policy rate may be on the high side, leaving room for cuts. Rising government bond yields have done much of the tightening. President Lagarde will step down in February 2027. We expect the inflation outlook and economic development to remain decisive for monetary policy, although ECB interpretation and communication may change depending on the composition of the Governing Council.

articles.title: The Riksbank and US midterm elections in focus
articles.heading: The Week Ahead
articles.fulltext:
A very interesting week coming up! The midterm elections, an expected Riksbank hike on Wednesday and Swedish and euro area inflation data will keep us busy. In Norway, Norges Bank is expected to keep rates unchanged amid continued inflation uncertainty.
US:
Midterm elections will be the main event and whether Democrats will reach a majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. A likely shift in the House will deadlock fiscal policy and increase pressures to negotiate budget issues. With control of the House, Democrats can force votes on legislation, but they cannot overcome the President’s veto. The President largely retains control of immigration, trade and foreign policy. We will also get key data including ISM manufacturing and services and non-farm payrolls. The US Treasury will announce its quarterly refunding plans.
Euro area: 
Euro area HICP inflation is the key event. Industrial production data for major economies and retail sales for Germany will also be of interest. The ECB wage tracker will be closely watched for signs of second-round effects from higher energy prices. Finally, German industrial orders could shed some light on production in the near term.
Sweden:
A very interesting week with the Riksbank’s rate decision on Wednesday and flash CPI on Thursday. On Friday we receive the final monthly budget balance ahead of the NDO’s forecast on November 26, and on Tuesday there will be a vote in parliament on the Center leader as Prime Minister, which is widely expected to fail.
Norway:
Norges Bank is widely expected to leave its policy rate unchanged at 4.50% at its upcoming rate decision. We expect the Bank to emphasise continued uncertainty around underlying inflation and the risk that elevated external price pressures could slow disinflation, while offering little clues to further guidance. As this is an interim decision, no new projections will be published. Existing home prices have recovered some of the weakness over the summer, although the 3m/3m trend remains broadly flat. We expect modest gains towards year-end and price growth of 3.0% in 2026. Manufacturing production is likely to rebound in September following the previous month’s decline.
